The most frequently cited concern was safety and security (16.8%), encompassing worries about the security of personal belongings left behind and the potential for civil disorder if a person were to relocate during a grid outage. Other top concerns included transportation and mobility (13.1%), availability of resources and supplies (12.6%), and pets (12.0%), with many stating they would not relocate without their animals. These responses underscore that shared resilience infrastructure must address these functional and psychological barriers, or the City could invest in creating resilience hubs that go unutilized. Further data detailing community requests for emergency government planners emphasized both micro-level preparedness needs and macro-level infrastructure demands. Residents requested more specific information regarding how the City would communicate in a disaster/grid outage, where shelter locations would be located, and how residents lacking personal vehicles would be transported. Although most of the community-based research focused on individual experiences, impacts of outages, and preparedness actions, technical demands were vocalized, including the need for “more utility power redundancy—more power lines, local generation sources, and microgrids, plus more non-fossil fuel energy.” Other requests focused on prioritizing evacuation and support for “elderly and people with disabilities,” and providing location-specific, hour- by-hour guides for response. Following the tabletop exercises, focus groups, canvasses, and survey research, the CSG integrated community concerns with the disruption scenarios established by the CIT. Initially it was assumed that the disaster scenarios would be the foundation of the 17 minimum resilience standards, for example a minimum resilience standard would be created for heat events, rain events, etc. Although this was the case for some of the minimum resilience standards, the CSG determined that other standards should focus on particular vulnerabilities, no matter the context of the grid outage, and on specific negative impacts, no matter the vulnerable group or outage context. The resulting minimum resilience standards developed under F3 establish a critical, community-centric baseline for energy resilience planning. These standards move beyond typical critical infrastructure protection by defining the functional necessities required by residents during extended grid disruptions. The minimum resilience standards do not serve as a community mandate but a conceptual framework to prioritize program design and implementation. The framework provides the structure for ongoing cumulative impact work of CIT and Community Stakeholder Group members. Grid outage/disaster scenario-based minimum resilience standards included extreme cold, extreme heat, and rain events/flooding. Addressing Duluth's cold-climate reality, the Winter Conditions - Extreme Cold standard requires that all community members possess an emergency plan for power outages during extreme cold, incorporating at- home options (like reducing drafts with DIY weatherization and using warm clothes) and providing clear relocation information. The Summer Conditions - Extreme Heat standard mandates that community members understand heat impacts and have a plan for adequate cooling, either at home or at community-based cooling centers. Shared solutions prioritize the use of cooling centers, giving vulnerable populations and those experiencing heat-related illnesses priority access.
